passage:
At the park in Osaka, a smiling woman on a bench held out a pink sweet. "Want one?" Yuki, five, trotted toward her at once.
"Yuki, come back to me," called Aiko, his mother, catching his hand. "We don't take sweets from people we don't know." The woman nodded and put it away.
Later the wind blew Yuki's hat under a hedge. A tall park keeper in a grey coat, face serious, pulled it out and held it up. Yuki hid behind Aiko's legs.
"He works here, see his badge?" Aiko said softly. Yuki peeked, grabbed the hat and whispered, "Thank you."

qa.q: What did the woman on the bench hold out?
qa.a: A pink sweet.

qa.q: Why did Yuki trot toward the smiling woman but hide from the park keeper?
qa.a: The smile and the pink sweet felt nice, so she seemed safe, while the keeper's serious face made Yuki nervous, even though he was the one helping.

qa.q: What rule did Aiko use, and why does it suit a five-year-old?
qa.a: We don't take sweets from people we don't know; a simple rule protects Yuki when a nice feeling might make him trust too quickly.

qa.q: How might the park keeper feel when Yuki hides?
qa.a: He might feel a little sad, or be used to it, and glad when Yuki finally whispers thank you.

grounding: A five-year-old heads straight for a smiling stranger with a sweet but hides from a serious-looking park keeper who is helping him.

passage:
In the kindergarten garden, Vikas spotted shiny red berries on a hedge. "Sweets!" he said, and reached out.
"Stop, Vikas." Miss Fernandes knelt beside him. "Those aren't for eating. We only eat food from our tiffin or from grown-ups we know."
Near the gate, Deepak Bhaiya, the school caretaker with a big moustache and a mop, bent down. "Your lace is open, little one."
Vikas scrunched his face and ran back to Miss Fernandes, clutching her dupatta.
"That's Deepak Bhaiya. He helps us every day," she said. "Shall we let him tie it together?"
Vikas held her hand tight and stuck out one foot.

qa.q: What did Vikas spot on the hedge?
qa.a: Shiny red berries.

qa.q: Why did the berries seem good to Vikas but Deepak Bhaiya seem scary?
qa.a: The berries looked like sweets, so they felt nice and safe, while the big moustache and mop made him nervous, though Deepak Bhaiya only wanted to help.

qa.q: How did Miss Fernandes handle each of Vikas's feelings?
qa.a: She stopped the berries with a clear rule, and with the caretaker she named him and stayed close so Vikas could accept help while feeling safe.

qa.q: What might Deepak Bhaiya think when Vikas runs away?
qa.a: He may feel a little hurt, or be used to it, and patient enough to wait while the teacher introduces him.

grounding: A kindergarten child reaches for sweet-looking berries but runs from a kind caretaker, because nice and nervous feelings decide what seems safe.

passage:
I'm Irfan, and on Sunday I took my little brother Abhinav to the fair with Ammi.
A man in a sparkly hat was giving out free candyfloss near the back gate. Abhinav let go of my hand and ran straight to him. I caught up and pulled him back to Ammi.
Later he got lost for a minute near the swings. A lady at the help desk, in a plain brown sweater, knelt and asked his name. Abhinav screamed and wouldn't answer until Ammi came running.
I don't know exactly what he was thinking. Maybe sparkly felt friendly and plain felt scary. Now we practise who to ask for help.

qa.q: What was the man near the back gate giving out?
qa.a: Free candyfloss.

qa.q: What might explain why Abhinav ran to one stranger but screamed at the other?
qa.a: The sparkly hat and candyfloss probably felt fun and friendly, while the plain helper felt strange and scary, so his feelings decided who seemed safe.

qa.q: What could Ammi and Irfan practise with Abhinav?
qa.a: Staying with the grown-up he came with, and if he is lost, going to a help desk or staff member instead of whoever looks fun.

qa.q: How did Irfan probably feel when Abhinav let go and ran?
qa.a: A jolt of worry and responsibility, which is why Irfan ran to catch up and bring Abhinav back to Ammi.

grounding: An older sibling sees a young child run to a sparkly stranger with candyfloss yet scream at a plainly dressed help-desk worker.

passage:
Tuesday: At the colony park, a smiling man held out a pink lollipop. Tenzin, five, ran straight to him. His aunt Nirmala hurried over and took his hand. "We don't take sweets from people we don't know." Tenzin pouted. "But he smiled."
Thursday: The new bus helper, a tall aunty with a plain grey sari and no smile, reached for his bag. Tenzin hid behind Nirmala and cried.
Next Monday: The same helper knelt and tied his loose shoelace. Tenzin peeked at her, then held out his hand to climb in.

qa.q: What did the smiling man hold out to Tenzin?
qa.a: A pink lollipop.

qa.q: Why did Tenzin cry when the bus helper reached for his bag?
qa.a: Tenzin felt scared because she looked plain and did not smile, even though she was there to help.

qa.q: What did Nirmala do well when Tenzin ran to the stranger?
qa.a: She hurried over, took his hand and calmly said they don't take sweets from people they don't know.

qa.q: How might the bus helper feel when Tenzin hides from her?
qa.a: She might feel a little sad or patient, knowing children need time, which is why she knelt to tie his shoelace later.

grounding: Over several days a young boy trusts a smiling stranger and fears a plain-looking helper, guided by how each makes him feel.

passage: The Kolkata station was packed and noisy, and Papa, Manoj, was stuck in a long ticket queue. Siddharth, five, held the bag strap. A man with a shiny red balloon bent down, smiling. "Want to see the big engine?" Siddharth let go of the strap. Papa turned just then, dropped out of the queue, and scooped him up. "We stay together. Always." Later a lady from the help desk, in a plain blue uniform, came to check on them. Siddharth buried his face in Papa's shirt and would not look at her.

qa.q: What did the man with the balloon ask Siddharth?
qa.a: "Want to see the big engine?"

qa.q: Why did Siddharth let go of the bag strap?
qa.a: The shiny balloon and the smiling man felt nice and exciting, so Siddharth felt safe going with him.

qa.q: What choice did Papa make when he saw the man, and why was it right?
qa.a: He left the queue at once and picked Siddharth up, because staying together mattered more than the tickets.

qa.q: How might the help-desk lady feel when Siddharth hides from her?
qa.a: She may understand that he's scared and tired, even though she came to help, and keep her distance kindly.

grounding: At a crowded station a young boy is drawn to a smiling stranger and hides from a plain-looking helper, judging by feelings.

passage:
Monday: At the park, a smiling man held out a toffee. "Come, see my puppies in the car." Omkar ran toward him. Aai caught his hand and walked him straight to the park guard, who went to find the man.
Wednesday: The new school-van helper, Saurabh uncle, had a big moustache and no smile. Omkar hid behind Aai and cried.
Friday: Omkar's shoe fell under the van seat. Saurabh uncle crawled in and found it. "Thank you," Omkar whispered.

qa.q: Who did Aai take Omkar to at the park?
qa.a: She walked him straight to the park guard.

qa.q: Why was Omkar scared of Saurabh uncle but happy to run to the smiling man?
qa.a: The smiling man and the toffee felt nice, so Omkar felt safe, while the big moustache and no smile made him feel frightened, even though Saurabh uncle was the real helper.

qa.q: How could Aai help Omkar with strangers after Monday?
qa.a: She could teach a simple rule: only go with grown-ups Aai or the school says are safe, however nice they seem.

qa.q: How might Saurabh uncle feel when a child hides and cries from him?
qa.a: He might feel a little sad or awkward, and pleased on Friday when Omkar finally whispered thank you.

grounding: Shows a young child trusting a smiling stranger with a sweet and fearing a plain-faced helper, guided only by how each one feels.

passage: The fair was so crowded that Shankar lost Papa's hand near the giant wheel. A man with a shiny red balloon bent down and smiled. "Come with me, I'll find your papa." Shankar reached for the balloon. Then a woman in a plain khaki jacket stepped between them. "I'm Devika, from the lost-children desk." Her face was stern. Shankar burst into tears and tried to pull away. Devika knelt and stayed beside him. She called out his name on the loudspeaker, and told the fair police about the balloon man. Papa came running. Shankar still thought the balloon man was nicer.

qa.q: What colour was the balloon the man held?
qa.a: It was a shiny red balloon.

qa.q: Why did Shankar reach for the balloon and cry when Devika came?
qa.a: The shiny balloon and the smile made Shankar feel happy and safe, while Devika's stern face made him feel afraid, so his feelings pointed him the wrong way.

qa.q: What could Papa tell Shankar after the fair?
qa.a: Papa could say that helpers at the desk are safe to go to even if they look serious, and never to go with someone who just offers a treat.

qa.q: How might Devika feel when a lost child cries at her?
qa.a: She might feel sorry he is scared but stay calm, because she knows keeping him with her is what keeps him safe.

grounding: Shows a young child in a crowd trusting a smiling stranger with a balloon and fearing a plain-looking helper because of how each one makes him feel.

passage: In the garden of their Chennai apartment block, Anand found a bush with shiny purple berries. "They look like sweets!" He reached for one. "Don't touch, kanna!" boomed Karthik anna, the night watchman. Anand jumped. Karthik anna was big and never smiled, and Anand always crossed to the other side of the gate. He ran home crying. "He shouted at me, and the berries were so pretty." Amma hugged him. "Anna shouted to keep you safe. Pretty things are not always good to eat. Next time, ask me first." Anand thought about it. He still liked the berries better than Karthik anna.

qa.q: What did Anand find in the garden?
qa.a: A bush with shiny purple berries.

qa.q: Why did Anand think the berries were good and Karthik anna was bad?
qa.a: The berries looked pretty and sweet, so they felt safe, while Karthik anna's loud voice and big, unsmiling face made Anand feel scared.

qa.q: What simple rule did Amma give Anand, and why does it help at his age?
qa.a: Ask Amma first before eating something he finds; it is easy to remember and doesn't rely on how things look.

qa.q: How might Karthik anna see what happened in the garden?
qa.a: He probably felt worried when he saw Anand reaching for the berries, and may not know his loud voice frightens Anand.

grounding: Shows a young child trusting pretty berries because they look sweet and fearing a plain-looking watchman who was actually protecting him.

passage:
It was Durga Puja, and the pandal was crowded and bright.

"Ammi, that uncle has sweets!" said Arnab, five, pulling away. A smiling man in a shiny kurta was waving at him.

Hafsa held his hand tight. "We don't take sweets from people we don't know."

"But he's nice! He's smiling!"

"Smiling doesn't tell us who is safe."

Later, Arnab lost his slipper. A plain-looking volunteer in a grey shirt picked it up. Arnab hid behind Hafsa.

"He's the helper, beta. See his badge?"

Arnab peeked out and took the slipper.

qa.q: What was the volunteer wearing?
qa.a: A grey shirt.

qa.q: Why did Arnab want to go to the man with sweets?
qa.a: The man's smile and sweets gave Arnab a happy, trusting feeling, so he felt the man must be nice.

qa.q: What did Hafsa do to keep Arnab safe and help him understand?
qa.a: She held his hand, said they don't take sweets from strangers, and pointed out the volunteer's badge as a real sign of a helper.

qa.q: How might the volunteer feel when Arnab hid from him?
qa.a: The volunteer might feel a little sad or amused, knowing small children judge by looks.

grounding: A young child trusts a smiling stranger with sweets and fears a plain-looking helper, as feelings guide his judgments.

passage:
Kindergarten note, Christmas fair day, by the class teacher.

At the fair, Mohit, five, ran to a stall with bright pink cupcakes covered in sprinkles. He wanted to eat three. But he refused the plain banana bread that Sarika's mother had baked, saying, "It looks yucky."

Later, a new school guard with a stern face offered to help him find the bathroom. Mohit started to cry and clung to me.

I held his hand and introduced him to the guard by name. We talked about how the guard keeps everyone safe. I also let him taste a tiny piece of banana bread. He ate it all. 🎄

qa.q: What did Mohit say about the banana bread?
qa.a: "It looks yucky."

qa.q: Why did Mohit cry when the guard offered help?
qa.a: The guard's stern face made Mohit feel scared, so he judged the guard as unsafe, even though the guard was helping.

qa.q: What did the teacher do to help Mohit, and why was it useful?
qa.a: The teacher introduced the guard by name and explained the guard's job, and let Mohit taste the bread, so his feelings could be checked against what was real.

qa.q: How might Sarika's mother feel if she heard her bread looked yucky?
qa.a: She might feel a little hurt at first, then amused when Mohit ate it all.

grounding: A teacher notes a young child who trusts bright food and fears a stern-looking helper, as feelings guide his judgments.

passage:
The village fair came after the harvest, when the fields were bare and gold. Jatin, four, held his grandfather Yusuf's finger.

A man with a painted face and a big grin held out a balloon. "Come, come, little one!"

Jatin let go of Yusuf's finger and ran toward him.

Yusuf caught him quickly. "Stay with me, Jatin."

At the next stall, an old woman selling bangles, with a tired face and no smile, offered Jatin a small toy. He hid behind Yusuf's leg.

"She's our neighbour, Kamla Amma. You know her," Yusuf said gently.

Jatin peeked, then took the toy.

qa.q: What did the man with the painted face hold out?
qa.a: A balloon.

qa.q: Why did Jatin run toward the man with the balloon?
qa.a: The painted face and big grin made Jatin feel happy and excited, so the man seemed safe to him.

qa.q: What did Yusuf do that kept Jatin safe?
qa.a: He caught Jatin quickly, told him to stay close, and later reminded him that the old woman was a known neighbour.

qa.q: How might Kamla Amma feel when Jatin hid behind Yusuf?
qa.a: Kamla Amma might feel a bit sad or amused, since she was only being kind.

grounding: A young child runs to a smiling stranger and hides from a plain-faced neighbour, as feelings guide his judgment.

passage: At the June festival in their town square in Brazil, Paulo loved the man in the bright clown hat. The man smiled, gave Paulo a sweet, and said, "Come see the puppies behind the van." Paulo took a step. Leila, the grey-aproned lady at the corn stall, called, "Paulo, wait!" He hid behind a post; her plain face and loud voice scared him. Leila held his hand firmly and walked him straight to Mamãe. Mamãe hugged him tight and told the festival guard about the man. That night she said, "Nice smiles don't mean safe. Safe grown-ups bring you back to me."

qa.q: What did the man offer to show Paulo?
qa.a: The puppies behind the van.

qa.q: Why did Paulo trust the man in the clown hat but hide from Leila?
qa.a: The smile and the sweet made Paulo feel happy and safe, while Leila's plain face and loud voice made him nervous, so his feelings decided for him.

qa.q: What did the adults do right?
qa.a: Leila took Paulo straight to Mamãe, Mamãe told the festival guard at once, and that night she taught him that safe grown-ups bring you back to your parent.

qa.q: How might Leila have felt when Paulo hid from her?
qa.a: She was probably alarmed for his safety and maybe a little hurt, but she acted anyway, holding his hand and bringing him to Mamãe.

grounding: A young child trusts a friendly-seeming stranger because it feels good and fears a plain-looking helper because she makes him nervous.

passage: At the preschool Diwali party, a shiny box of bright pink sweets sat on the gate wall. Nobody knew who had left it. Chetan reached for one. "They look yummy, so they're good!" The new helper, Kashish didi, in her plain brown sari, gently moved the box away. Chetan stepped back, nervous; she didn't smile much, and her voice was deep. But she knelt and offered him a laddoo from the class tray. "These are from your teacher's kitchen. Those, we don't know." Chetan took it slowly. At pickup, the teacher told all the parents about the unknown box.

qa.q: Where was the shiny box of sweets?
qa.a: On the gate wall.

qa.q: Why did Chetan feel nervous of Kashish didi?
qa.a: Her plain sari, few smiles and deep voice made him uneasy, so his feeling said she wasn't safe even though she was helping him.

qa.q: What rule did Kashish didi show?
qa.a: Eat food from people we know, not food from an unknown giver, however nice it looks; she explained it kindly and offered a safe laddoo.

qa.q: What is it like for Kashish didi when Chetan steps back?
qa.a: She may feel a little sad at seeming scary, but she stays gentle and kneels to his level.

grounding: A young child judges sweets as safe because they look nice, and a plain-looking helper as scary because he feels nervous.

passage:
Monday, a cold winter morning: Tarun cries at the bus stop. The new attendant, Jatin bhaiya, is tall and unsmiling, with a scratchy voice. "Scary!" Tarun says.
Wednesday: At the park, a smiling man in a cartoon sweater offers Tarun a toffee. Tarun beams and reaches out. Mumma steps in, says, "No, thank you," and takes Tarun home. She tells the park guard that afternoon.
Saturday: Mumma plays "safe or not" with Tarun. "Who helped you with your bag on the bus?" "Jatin bhaiya." "Do we know him?" "Yes!" "And the toffee man?" Tarun thinks. "Smiley, but we don't know him."

qa.q: What did the man in the cartoon sweater offer Tarun?
qa.a: A toffee.

qa.q: Why did Tarun call Jatin bhaiya scary?
qa.a: Tarun felt nervous because Jatin bhaiya was tall and unsmiling with a scratchy voice; the feeling made him seem unsafe even though he helped.

qa.q: What helped Tarun learn?
qa.a: Mumma stepping in at the park, telling the guard that afternoon, and playing "safe or not" to link safety to knowing someone, not to smiles.

qa.q: What might Jatin bhaiya feel when Tarun cries at the bus stop?
qa.a: He might feel a bit hurt or awkward, though he keeps helping Tarun with the bag.

grounding: A young child feels a smiling stranger is safe and a plain-looking helper is scary, until a parent helps him sort it out.

passage:
The Diwali mela was packed and deafening. "Harish, hold my hand!" Devika shouted.
But Harish saw a smiling man with shiny balloons and a bag of sweets. "He's nice!" Harish said, and let go.
Devika, his mother, caught his hand in two steps and pulled him close. "We don't go to people we don't know, even smiley ones."
Near the gate sat a plain-looking woman in a grey uniform at the lost-children desk. Harish hid behind Devika's legs. "She looks scary."
Devika knelt. "She's a helper. If you're ever lost, she's the one to go to."

qa.q: Where did the woman in the grey uniform sit?
qa.a: Near the gate, at the lost-children desk.

qa.q: Why did Harish let go of Devika's hand for the man with balloons?
qa.a: The shiny balloons and sweets gave him a happy, excited feeling, so the man felt nice and safe to him.

qa.q: What could Devika do before the next crowded fair?
qa.a: She could show Harish the helper desk first and practise together: if lost, go to someone in uniform at the desk, never to anyone offering treats.

qa.q: What was it like for Devika when Harish let go?
qa.a: She was frightened for a moment, which is why she caught him in two steps and held him close.

grounding: Shows a young child trusting a friendly-seeming stranger because it feels good and fearing a plain-looking helper, with his mother stepping in.
